B2B software is fragmenting. The cost barrier that forced buyers into generic tools is collapsing, and AI is what breaks it.

## Most B2B Software Is Generic by Necessity

For most of the last 20 years, the SaaS model worked like this: build once, sell to many. The economics required it. Custom software was expensive. The more a vendor could standardize their product, the more customers they could serve without proportionally growing their engineering team.

That constraint shaped everything. Most B2B buyers learned to accept software that almost fit. They hired consultants to bridge the gap. They built spreadsheets to handle edge cases. They paid for features they didn't use and worked around the ones they needed.

## A Framework for Thinking About It

Two axes matter when evaluating business software:

- **Bespoke vs. Productized:** Built specifically for this customer, or off-the-shelf?
- **Flexible vs. Guided:** Does it enforce a workflow, or leave structure to the user?

<SaasQuadrant client:load era="before" title="The SaaS Landscape" />

Most enterprise SaaS lives in the bottom-right: Workflow Software. Productized and guided. Shopify, Salesforce, industry-specific ERPs. These are the systems that run most businesses.

The top-right quadrant — Adaptive Systems — is what every sophisticated buyer actually wants. Software that enforces structured workflows but is built specifically for how their business operates. Historically, only the largest enterprises could afford it. Everyone else compromised.

## The Precursor: Low-Code Tools

The demand was always there. Retool and Airtable took this problem on.

At a $50M ARR manufacturing marketplace, we replaced purpose-built SaaS tools with Retool and Airtable workflows. Not because we preferred them. Because the off-the-shelf options didn't fit, and these let us build something closer to what we actually needed without a full engineering cycle.

The result was clumsy. Retool requires a developer. Airtable breaks at scale. The UX is obviously stitched together. But we got workflows that matched our operations instead of the reverse.

That's the demand signal. Companies will put up with clumsy tools to get something that fits. The question was always whether something cleaner was possible.

## AI Changes the Build Economics

The cost to move from productized to bespoke has dropped sharply. A small team can now build a guided, workflow-enforcing system tailored to a specific customer's operations at a fraction of what it cost three years ago.

This doesn't mean SaaS is going away. It means the category is fragmenting. Buyers who accepted generic tools because bespoke was unaffordable now have options. Builders who needed large engineering teams to serve them don't.

The result is hyper-verticalization: software built for smaller and smaller customer segments, with tighter structural fit to how each segment actually operates. In the limit, personalization for each customer.

<SaasQuadrant client:load era="after" title="The Shift" />

## My Test

I'm building ERPForge to test this directly. The hypothesis: an AI-assisted ERP that adapts to a specific company's operations, at a build cost that makes it viable for small and mid-sized manufacturers.

Retool and Airtable took this problem on. The question is whether AI gets the rest of the way — where the new floor on build cost lands, and whether the resulting product is structurally strong enough to support real operations or just a cleaner version of the same clumsy workaround.

## The Barbarian's Advantage

During an [interview on the Y Combinator Startup Podcast](https://open.spotify.com/podcast-chapter/032tMsS7qGoi2qhCryN71f?si=1664b2ac644b461e&nd=1&dlsi=8981c818af6a46e4), Claude Code creator Boris Cherny talked about a bug he was working on. He approached it like a typical Senior Software Engineer, following good investigation and script practices to diagnose and solve the bug. He gave it to his coworker who just told Claude Code to "solve the bug". Claude Code used some of the same methods to tackle the problem and solved it while he could not.

He then went on to talk about the beginner's advantage. A beginner in a changing industry is not accustomed to the old ways, so they see newer ways as the path to solve most problems.

Before I hear Boris put a name to this advantage, I thought of it as the "barbarian approach". Coming from software development where strong coding practices were enforced and developers could explain their approaches, I felt a bit like a barbarian trying to build similar software without the tools they had in their belts.

That led me to re-explore the findings of the book "Barbarians at the Gate", telling the tale of RJR Nabisco and the degradation of the ownership moat through new financial takeover vehicles.

## The Original Barbarians

In 1988, KKR bought RJR Nabisco for $25 billion. They didn't know how to run a tobacco-and-food conglomerate. They didn't need to.

What made the deal possible wasn't operational expertise. It was a new class of financial instrument. Michael Milken's junk bond network gave firms like KKR access to capital structures that turned $15 million in equity into multi-billion-dollar acquisitions. The leverage ratio was absurd. The playbook was simple: find an undervalued company, load it with debt, extract value.

Most of those firms weren't better operators. Many failed. But enough succeeded to permanently change how corporate America thought about defensibility. The moat wasn't ownership anymore. It was whether you could actually run the business once you had it.

## The New Leverage

AI development tools (Lovable, Cursor, Claude, v0) are doing to software what junk bonds did to acquisitions. They're not making everyone a software engineer. They're giving people who understand business logic the ability to build without one.

That distinction matters. The bottleneck in most SaaS platforms was never the individual transaction logic. It's straightforward. The complexity is in encoding thousands of business rules, edge cases, and operational workflows into code. That required teams of engineers who often didn't fully understand the domain, translating requirements from people who did.

Now the people who understand the business logic can write the rules themselves. Not all of them. Not perfectly. But enough to get 70% of the way to a working platform in days instead of months.

<LeverageShift client:load title="The Translation Layer Collapses" />

And that changes the math on whether to attempt the other 30%.

## What Still Holds

Distribution. Sales teams. Network effects. Regulatory compliance. Data moats built on years of customer activity. DevOps at scale. None of these get easier because someone can prompt their way to a working prototype.

The barbarians of the 1980s still had to operate the companies they bought. Many couldn't. Building the platform is becoming the easy part. Running it, selling it, and scaling it still require everything they always did.

## The Shift

KKR didn't win every deal. They didn't need to. They changed the game by making it possible to *try*. Incumbents who had coasted on the sheer difficulty of replication suddenly had to defend on merit.

AI tools won't topple every SaaS company. But they're about to increase the number of credible attackers, lower the cost of each attempt, and expose which systems were only defensible because they were expensive to rebuild.

## The Thesis Test

[Sample ERP](/work/sample-erp) proved a product leader with the right process can direct AI tools to build a system that holds to real architectural discipline. But the rigor lived in *me*: the discovery questions I knew to ask, the order I asked them in, the judgment calls translating answers into architecture decisions.

ERPForge is the harder question: can that judgment be codified into reusable AI skills, so the next custom system builds faster than the last, and the one after that faster still? If yes, the skills become the product. The ERP is just what they produce.

I think of this as trying to build a software factory: not one custom ERP, but a repeatable line that takes a specific business's requirements in one end and turns out working software on the other, without a systems integrator standing in the middle for months. A factory doesn't get slower as it makes more units. The test is whether custom software delivery can work the same way.

## The Problem

Traditional ERPs exist because code was expensive. Vendors built lowest-common-denominator software for a business segment, then tried to configure it per customer. Big customers got the most features. Small ones got the base package or cobbled together Excel and point solutions.

Custom systems, built to match how a specific business actually operates, used to require a systems integrator: weeks of discovery, a proposal, a build. The discovery process itself, knowing which questions unlock the right configuration, is where most of that time and cost goes.

## The Approach

ERPForge is a set of Claude skills that encode a product consultant's discovery process, not a single ERP build:

- **`/design-review`** structured 10-section review before writing any code
- **Discovery templates** 80 questions across 12 categories for BOM and product scoping
- **`/write-docs`** auto-generates API reference, migration guides, and changelogs

The BOM rebuild on Sample ERP is where this got tested first. I gave Claude context on typical BOM structures and manufacturing processes, gave it the discovery skill, and had it interview me about product workflows and configurations. It rebuilt the data model from those answers. Four hours from kickoff to a restructured, production-ready BOM system, work that would normally take a systems integrator weeks.

The demo at erpforge.kyle-mcleod.io runs that discovery-to-spec flow directly: it interviews a user about their manufacturing operation and produces a structured spec and BOM configuration, the same judgment calls I made manually on Sample ERP, run through the skill instead of through me.

## What's Actually Hard

Encoding a consultant's judgment is slower than writing code. A good product consultant doesn't just ask questions, they know which questions unlock the right configuration, in what order, and how to translate the answer into an architecture decision. Getting explicit about knowledge that usually lives in someone's head, and reliable enough that Claude runs it consistently, is most of the actual work.

The demo proves the discovery-to-spec flow works. It doesn't yet close the loop into a build. That's the next milestone: full interview, build, and iteration without manual orchestration in between.

## What This Proves (So Far)

The discovery skill reliably turns a structured interview into a usable spec. That's phase one, and it's live now. It's the input side of the factory: turning a business's specific requirements into something a build can run on, without me in the loop translating.

Phase two is closing the loop: automating interview → build → iterate so the skill doesn't just produce a spec, it produces a working system. That's the difference between "I can build an ERP fast" and an actual software factory, where a product consultant's tooling can deliver a custom ERP to a manufacturer without the delivery time growing with each new customer. The bet is that the gap between "expert needed" and "anyone with domain knowledge can" keeps closing as the skills get better.

import BuildTimeline from '../../components/BuildTimeline.tsx'; [See how the planner works →](#plan-workflow) ## The Thesis Test The original version of this page asked whether AI tools could produce product depth at prototype speed. That was the right question for a four-hour demo. It's not the right question anymore. catch.ai has become a real application I use every time I plan a trip: authentication, a proper data model, external integrations, a working mobile UI. The question worth asking now is what a product leader learns by building *and using* a complete personal application with AI, past the point where a demo has to hold up. The answer so far: AI is most useful inside traditional software when it translates ambiguous human input into structured action, synthesizes multiple sources of context, or helps a user make a decision. Everything around that still depends on ordinary product work — data models, integrations, permissions, reliability. That's a different, and more useful, finding than "AI can build a demo fast." ## The Problem Fishing trips generate useful information. Where I went, what the conditions were, what worked. I was tracking it across four disconnected tools: handwritten notes, Google Maps pins, manually pulled USGS stream data, and a general AI chat for pattern questions. None of it added up to a usable history or a repeatable way to plan the next trip. catch.ai brings those pieces together. It records what happened, enriches each spot and trip with environmental context, and uses that history to help decide what to do next. ## The Core Loop: Remember → Understand → Plan **Remember.** Voice input converted into structured trip and catch records. Persistent drafts survive an interrupted session on the river. Catches link to species, tackle, and spots, and past trips edit through the same flow used to log a new one. **Understand.** Saved spots connect to map pins and the right USGS or NOAA stations. Flow, gage height, tide, and forecast data sit alongside each spot's trip history, so a spot means more than a pin on a map.
**Plan.** Start from a saved spot or describe a new trip conversationally. The app proposes grounded options, layers in conditions and forecast, generates a structured day plan, and saves it as an upcoming trip rather than leaving it in a chat window.
## Inside the Trip Planner The planner isn't a chatbot bolted onto the app. It's a pattern worth more attention than the fishing use case: take an ambiguous goal, turn it into grounded options, let the user choose or refine, enrich the choice with real context, and convert the decision into a structured record the rest of the product can use. {/* TODO: screenshots of the conversational and guided planning paths once available */} The flow, in both entry points: 1. The user states intent, either by describing a trip conversationally or picking a saved spot. 2. AI proposes candidate options grounded against real place data, not generated coordinates. 3. The user selects, rejects, or refines the set. 4. The app pulls in live conditions, forecast, and (for saved spots) prior history. 5. AI assembles a structured, time-blocked plan and saves it as a real trip record. The conversational path adds a step at the front, geocoding AI-suggested place names against a maps API rather than trusting generated coordinates directly. The guided path skips straight to structured selectors since the location is already known. Either way, the conversation is one part of the workflow. Maps, verified place data, environmental APIs, and the trip system of record do the rest. ## Why This Matters for Commercial SaaS The pattern underneath the planner generalizes: **ambiguous intent → grounded options → human selection → external context → structured plan → persistent record.** That shows up constantly in commercial software, just with different nouns.

The lesson isn't "add AI chat." It's: use conversation where the problem is unclear, structured UI where the domain is known, deterministic tools to verify hard facts, and external or historical data to ground the decision. Then save the result into the product's existing workflow instead of leaving it in the chat window. ## From Four-Hour Demo to Working Product The first version of catch.ai took roughly four hours in Lovable and proved AI tools could move fast from product direction to a working interface. That was never the interesting part. The real work came after: rebuilding the data model, adding authentication and row-level security, integrating maps and environmental APIs, designing the mobile workflow, adding voice and vision features, and turning AI output into persistent product records. I still direct implementation almost entirely through AI tools. The experiment stopped being "can they generate a demo" a while ago. It's now whether I can use them to evolve a coherent product I actually rely on. ## What's Actually Hard **External data isn't product-ready data.** USGS, NOAA, and map services use different identifiers, coverage models, and failure modes. Making that useful took linking, caching, fallbacks, and plain-language interpretation, not just an API call. **AI suggestions need deterministic grounding.** The planner never trusts generated coordinates directly. It asks AI for a precise place name and resolves the pin with real geocoding. The same discipline matters anywhere a generated answer has to map to a real customer, SKU, or address. **Mobile platform details don't disappear.** Safari microphone permissions, safe areas, touch targets, and outdoor readability all needed direct attention. AI tooling doesn't remove platform constraints, it just moves them later. **Security is still manual work.** Authentication, row-level security, and demo-data isolation are conventional, necessary, and occasionally in tension with legitimate AI and voice workflows. **Context has to be a system, not a prompt.** Planning quality depends on structured history, saved spots, and current conditions. Better prompts can't substitute for a coherent data model underneath them. ## What This Demonstrates (So Far) AI-assisted tools can help a product leader build and evolve a real application across multiple workflows, integrations, and AI modalities, not just a single demo screen. The most valuable AI features here weren't standalone chat experiences. They worked best turning unstructured input into structured data, helping navigate an ambiguous choice, or synthesizing context into a decision, then handing the user back to a normal product workflow. catch.ai doesn't demonstrate enterprise scale or that one person can replace a software team. What it shows is a practical way to build deep enough, on something I actually use, to test real product decisions and learn implementation patterns that carry over to commercial software.

import BuildTimeline from '../../components/BuildTimeline.tsx'; ## The Thesis Test Most of my AI builds test speed: how much can one person ship, how fast. Sample ERP tests the opposite constraint. Manufacturing ERPs are unforgiving of sloppy architecture. Bad data models compound. A BOM structure that's wrong at month one is expensive to unwind at month six. So the question here wasn't "how fast can Claude Code build this," it was "will it hold to real architecture and engineering discipline when the domain punishes shortcuts." ## The Problem Traditional ERPs exist because code was expensive. Vendors built lowest-common-denominator software for a business segment, then tried to configure it per customer. Big customers got the most features. Small ones got the base package or cobbled together Excel and point solutions. At MacroFab, we built manufacturing workflows in-house because MRPs were expensive and slow to implement. The cost structure forced that tradeoff. Build it yourself or settle for software that doesn't match your operations. What if the cost structure changed, without giving up the rigor a real ERP needs? ## The Approach I architected the system with ChatGPT first. Talked through the design on a walk, generated a `CLAUDE.md` file and an architecture doc, then used Claude Code to build the full platform. Architecture and data modeling decisions were made deliberately, before a line of code existed, the same way I'd scope a system for an engineering team. - **Architecture first:** hosting, data model, and UI guidelines decided via ChatGPT before touching Claude Code - **Plan mode:** used to turn general business context into a concrete build plan before generating code - **BOM rebuild via discovery:** gave Claude context on manufacturing BOM structures, then had it interview me on real workflows and rebuild the data model against those answers, not assumptions The BOM rebuild is the clearest example of the discipline this tests. Recursive multi-level BOMs, revision control, alternate components: this is exactly the kind of data model that breaks under a "just make it work" approach. Four hours from kickoff to a restructured, production-ready BOM system, built to hold up under the domain's real constraints, not just demo well. ## What It Does Eight integrated modules: Products & BOM, Quotes, Orders, Inventory, Purchasing, Manufacturing, Shipping, and Invoices. The full quote-to-order-to-ship workflow runs end to end. The BOM system is the deepest module. Recursive multi-level BOMs with revision control, alternate components, CSV import with column auto-detection, and depth-first cost rollup through the full tree.
## What's Actually Hard Cloud hosting was new territory. A full day to get Railway + Cloudflare configured with containers, DNS, and security. That part had nothing to do with AI capability and everything to do with unfamiliar infrastructure. The harder question was whether Claude Code would cut corners on the data model once the domain got complicated. It didn't, but only because the architecture was scoped explicitly up front. Left to move fast on its own, AI tooling defaults to the quickest working version. Holding it to real engineering discipline took deliberate scoping, not just good prompts. ## What This Proves (So Far) A product leader with the right process can direct AI tools to build a system that holds to real architectural discipline, not just a fast demo. The rigor came from explicit upfront scoping and discovery, not from the tooling doing it automatically. That raises the actual question I care about next: if the discipline lives in the process, not the tool, can that process itself be turned into something repeatable? That's what [ERPForge](/work/erpforge) is testing: whether the discovery-and-architecture workflow that made this build hold together can be codified into reusable skills, so the next system builds faster without losing the rigor.
